messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have some trouble setting up a damped oscillator in deSolve. It seemed like a straightforward task, but I did not succeed …
The goal is to model following differential equation:
d2x/dt2 = eta*x + zeta*dx/dt 

(Quite similar to http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damping; it's a somewhat simplified version of the standard damped oscillator).

Any help is appreciated!
Felix

messages.body_plain:
Hello Felix,

You need to introduce new variable y=dx/dt  and your equation reads
dy/dt= eta*x + zeta*y.  So solution
will be for states (x, y) and paramaters (eta, zeta). Remember that
any higher order ODE can be expressed as first order.

Best,
-Mehmet

messages.body_plain:
On 12/6/2012 8:02 PM, Suzen, Mehmet wrote:
> Hello Felix,
>
> You need to introduce new variable y=dx/dt  and your equation reads
> dy/dt= eta*x + zeta*y.  So solution
> will be for states (x, y) and paramaters (eta, zeta). Remember that
> any higher order ODE can be expressed as first order.

Yes, right, cf. page 3+4 in:

http://journal.r-project.org/archive/2010-2/RJournal_2010-2_Soetaert~et~al.pdf


so you may get something like:

library(deSolve)

osci <- function (t, states, parms) {
   with(as.list(c(states,  parms)), {
     dx <- y
     dy <- -eta * x - zeta * y
     list(c(dx, dy))
   })
}

states <- c(x = 1, y = 0)
out <- ode(states, osci, times = 0:100,
   parms = c(eta = 0.2, zeta = 0.1))
plot(out)



Have fun!

Thomas P.

Hi Tom,

I don't have a ready made example at hand, but handling of lags resp.

messages.subject: [R-sig-dyn-mod] Failed attempt to use modFit- part 2
messages.subject_clean: [R-sig-dyn-mod] Failed attempt to use modFit- part 2
messages.body_plain:
Hello list:

A while back I asked a question about fitting population growth models to Venezuelan census data.  This post to the list is intended as a follow up to those questions, in case anyone is interested.  Once again, the census data and the R/simecol/FME code to fit to the generalized logistic growth model (as given in Petzoldt's "Konstruktion ökologischer Mo delle mit der Open Source Software R", page 55):

censos.csv-------------------------------------------------
"time"    "pob"
1873    1732411
1881    2005139
1891    2221572
1920    2479525
1926    2814131
1936    3364347
1941    3850771
1950    5034838
1961    7523999
1971    10721522
1981    14516735
1990    18105265
2001    23232553
2011    27150095
-----------------------------------------------------

library("simecol")
library("FME")

censo <- read.table("censos.csv",header=TRUE)

modelo_generalizado <- new("odeModel",
        main=function(time,init,parms, ...) {
            x <- init
            p <- parms
            dpob <- x["pob"]^p["alfa"]*p["r"]*(1-(x["pob"]/p["K"])^p["beta"])^p["gamma"]
            list(dpob)},
        init=c(pob=1732411),
        parms=c(r=1.488546e-08,K=64672787,alfa=1.943699,beta=1,gamma=4.223137),
        times=seq(from=1873,to=2011,by=1),
        solver="lsoda")

#función de costo
fCosto <- function(p) {
    parms(modelo_generalizado) <- p
    out <- out(sim(modelo_generalizado))
    return(modCost(out, censo, weight="std"))
}

#ajuste del modelo
resultado <- modFit(fCosto, parms(modelo_generalizado) )
parms(modelo_generalizado) <- resultado$par
parms(modelo_generalizado)
cat("SC : ",ssqOdeModel(NULL,modelo_generalizado,censo$time,censo[2]),"\n")

---------------------------------------

At that time, I had asked the reasons as to why the attempts to use FME's modFit had failed, giving the following error message: "need at least 2 non NA values to interpolate with approx".   simecol's fitOdeModel (using the PORT algorithm) worked only with specific choice of parameters and the rk family of solvers.

In a response, Thomas Petzoldt suggested running a test for simultanaeous identifiability of parameters and fixing some while fitting the others.  This I did and indeed, for the generalized logistic growth models, the collinearity is much much greater than 20, even when fixing the K parameter (asymptotic population level) based upon knowledge (guesswork, rather) of the population at inflexion point.  Still, I could not used modFit.

After banging my head against this problem for sometime, and even running the ode Model with the Euler method without using simecol, I realized that the problem was in this line:

            dpob <- x["pob"]^p["alfa"]*p["r"]*(1-(x["pob"]/p["K"])^p["beta"])^p["gamma"]

For some choice of parameters (while searching for the optimum parameter set), the current population at time t (x["pob"]) would exceed the K parameter and thus (1-(x["pob"]/p["K"])^p["beta"]) could take on negative values, which, when raised to a certain exponent p["gamma"]<1, would mean trouble, thus accounting for those NA values.

Of course, in theory x["pob"] would gradually increase towards K and would never surpass that level but when using numerical differential equation solvers ("lsoda", "rk", and the like) there was no guarantee that x["pob"] would not shoot past K.  So I patched the following fix in the main equation simecol slot:

            if (x["pob"]<=p["K"])
                dpob <- x["pob"]^p["alfa"]*p["r"]*(1-(x["pob"]/p["K"])^p["beta"])^p["gamma"]
            else
                dpob <- 0

Although now modFit works, its still a patch and it seems "artificial" because it's not the way the model was intended to be.  So my question now is: Is there any way to "tell" the deSolver in simecol that x["pob"] cannot shoot past K in the dpob differential equation?

Thanks and Regards,

jose loreto romero palma

P.S. Season's greetings and happy holidays.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

thanks for your detailed feedback and analysis. I rewrote your example a 
little bit using with() which may cost a little bit CPU time but 
increases readability.

The reason for your difficulties is the high collinearity. It can be 
seen when plotting simulation and data (see last two lines of example 
below).

The essential problem lies in the poor representation of the saturation 
K by the given data, because it is questionable how much the population 
will grow after the last point, so it is a model-specification problem 
(inadequate model given the data) and not just a technical issue.


Thomas P.





#####################################################################

library("simecol")
library("FME")

censo <- read.table("censos.csv",header=TRUE)

modelo_generalizado <- new("odeModel",
   main = function(time,init,parms, ...) {
       with(as.list(c(init, parms)), {
         if (pob < K)
             dpob <- pob ^ alfa * r *(1-(pob/K)^beta)^gamma
         else
             dpob <- 0

         list(dpob)
       })
   },
   init = c(pob=1732411),
   parms = c(r=1.488546e08, K=64672787,
     alfa=1.943699, beta=1,gamma=4.223137),
   times = seq(from=1873, to=2011, by=1),
   solver = "lsoda"
)

#función de costo
fCosto <- function(p) {
     parms(modelo_generalizado) <- p
     out <- out(sim(modelo_generalizado))
     return(modCost(out, censo, weight="std"))
}

#ajuste del modelo
resultado <- modFit(fCosto, parms(modelo_generalizado) )
parms(modelo_generalizado) <- resultado$par
parms(modelo_generalizado)
cat("SC : ",ssqOdeModel(NULL, modelo_generalizado, censo$time, 
censo[2]), "\n")

# plot the model
modelo_generalizado <- sim(modelo_generalizado)
plot(modelo_generalizado, obs=censo)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

here another ODE model that fits your data rather well. The approach 
uses deSolve without simecol. It applies a two-equation growth model
that splits the population in a non-reproducing and a an actively 
reproducing fraction.

Note also that the parameters are again highly correlated and that 
versions with fixed parameter "a" would also result in a plausible 
curves, but with very different r and K.


Thomas P.


##===================================================================

library(FME)
library(deSolve)

## model function
model <- function(t, y, p) {
   with(as.list(c(y, p)), {
     dy1 <- -a * y1               # "inactive" part of population
     dy2 <-  a * y1 + r * y2 * (1 - y2 / K)  # growing population
     list(c(dy1, dy2), pob = y1 + y2)        # total pop = y1 + y2
   })
}

## cost function
fCost <- function(p) {
   parms[names(p)] <- p    # "names" allow to fit parameter subsets
   out <- ode(init, times = censo$time, model, parms = parms)
   cost <- modCost(out, censo)
   cat(parms, " : ", cost$model, "\n")
   cost
}

## data set
censo <- read.table("censos.csv", header = TRUE)

init  <- c(y1 = 1732411, y2 = 0)
parms <- c(r = 0.05, K = 3.0e7, a = 0.001)
times <- 1873:2100

out <- ode(init, times, model, parms)

plot(censo, xlim = c(1850, 2100), ylim = c(0, 5e7))
lines(out[, 1], out[, 4]) ## initial parameters

##--------------------------------------------------------------------


## fit model (all parameters)
result <- modFit(fCost, p = parms[c("r", "K", "a")])

## alternative: leave "a" untouched
#result <- modFit(fCost, p = parms[c("r", "K")])

## retrieve and display parameters
(parms[names(coef(result))] <- coef(result))
deviance(result)

## simulate fitted model and plot results
out <- ode(init, times = 1873:2100, model, parms)
lines(out[, 1], out[, 4], col = "red")
legend("topright", lty = 1, col = c("black", "red"),
   legend = c("initial parms", "fitted"))

messages.body_plain:
Hello Thomas,

Thanks for your helpful feedback.  The model you propose is not good- it's excellent.  The following is a summary of the models I tested for this data:

                             Collinearity
Model                SC      with all parameters
---------------------------------------------
Malthus        0.5677005     NA
Verhulst       0.5677032     4.3
Richards       0.567703      15.4
Blumberg       0.05629742    20.4    (*)
Generalized    0.02591176    1495.1
2 var model    0.005744879   10.3  <-- best model

(*) This fit corresponds to a 4 parameter Blumberg model 
with K fixed according to supposition of inflexion point N_inf

Fit of Parameters

Model                r         K (maximum population)
-------------------------------------------------
Malthus        0.0197321       +oo                  (*)
Verhulst       0.01973206      89,219,750,000,000   (*)
Richards       0.01973206      394,641,100          (*)
Blumberg       1.488546e-08    64,672,787  (**)
Generalized    7.283825e-10    118,310,000 (**)
2 var model    5.021216e-02    35,805,760

(*)    The saturation point K for these models is unrealistically high. In the case of the Richards model, this saturation point would suppose a population density of 430.62 inhabitants per square kilometer, which, although possible, I would consider unsustainable for Venezuela (area of 916,445 square kilometers).
(**) Low fitted values of r are compensated by alpha values close to 2.

SC is the sum of squares weighed by std deviation goodness of fit meassure.  The proposed 2 variable model SC is 5 times lower than the Generalized model and has identifiable parameters.  Still, I have some questions regarding this 2 variable model:

(1) Could you point me to some literature (if there is any) regarding the proposed model for demographical dynamics? In there is no literature to your knowledge (and there certainly isn't to mine), how did you come up with this model?  I'm writing an academic paper on this and I really need to know who to cite. 

(2) From what I see, it is a 2 compartiment model where you call variable y1 the inactive population and y2 the active population.  I take it that "active" and "inactive" refer to concepts in the epidemological context, but what would their meaning be in a population growth census model?  "Active" as being the part of the population that is procreating offspring does not sound reasonable as an interpretation for this concept.
My guess is that maybe inactive refers to the part of the population that is living in pre-industrial conditions (in the context of the demographic transition theory).  The population then gradually shifts into a modern, urban lifestyle with lower mortality and fertility rates.  In Venezuela, there was a major malaria epidemic and economic depressions (resulting from low coffee prices which was Venezuela's main export before oil) during the 1891-1920 period. Since 1920, Venezuela became an oil-producing country and this brought about the modern age.
This is just my guess but since you proposed the model, perhaps you can clarify this point.

(3) Does this 2 variable model have an analytical solution? The analytical solution of y1 is easy enough- an exponentially decreasing function.  But the solution of y2 eludes me.  also, what would the analytical equation for the inflection point of the population be?

Again, thank you for your really valuable feedback.

Regards,

jose loreto romero palma

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

thanks for your extensive summary. Please note that emails containing 
only attachments are "scrubbed" by the mailing list software. Such 
messages are archived:

https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-sig-dynamic-models/attachments/20121230/cb578886/attachment.pl

... but may not be sent to all subscribers.


The 2 equation approach seems to be frequently used in the literature 
but is quite obvious:

dy1/dt = -a * y1 + (b1-d1) * y1
dy2/dt =  a * y1 + (b2-d2) * y2

For micro-organisms it may be assumed that sub-population y1 adapts to 
the medium and only y2 is growing.

One may also assume that birth (b) and death (d) rates of population y1 
are balanced (b1 - d1 = 0), so that its net growth rate r1 = 0 and can 
be omitted, while in population y2: r2 = (b2 - d2) > 0. The latter can 
now be replaced by a resource limitation term, extended by further 
stages, or simply be "cut off" with a logistic term:

dy1/dt = -a * y1
dy2/dt =  a * y1 + rmax * (1 - y2/K) * y2


A demographic interpretation may be found in Wikipedia:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic_transition

... but it is surely much more complex in reality - especially the 
mechanisms, and the value of K. So be careful with your interpretation.

Thomas P.
